title: New Video
prompt:
12‑second experimental typographic short on vintage 35mm film (1960s look), 4:3 aspect ratio, 24fps. Grainy color, soft halation, gate weave, dust, hairline scratches, subtle vignette, mild projector flicker.

Scene: A flat 2d vintage and worn surface. Minimal transparent celluloid textures randomly around the space.

Typography behavior (critical constraint): The screen repeatedly fills with floating words and single characters that appear and disappear at different intervals, like optical printing and cut‑and‑paste title cards. Every on‑screen character must be taken ONLY from the phrase:
Seul astre exact un livre
(No numbers, no punctuation, no accents, no extra letters—only these letters and spaces.)
The bursts should feel like anagram fragments: letters scatter, jitter, snap into partial clusters, then dissolve—sometimes forming readable fragments like “Seul”, “astre”, “exact”, “un”, “livre”, and sometimes dissolving into abstract letter clouds—always constrained to the same character set.

Timing / progression:

0–2s: Start from an empty surface. Projector flicker and dust; first faint letter ghosts begin to stutter in the air.

2–8s: Rapid waves of letters and word-fragments cover the frame, drifting in parallax over the loft—some projected onto the floor, some hovering in front of lens—appearing/disappearing with rhythmic jump cuts and optical jitter.

8–10s: The chaos subtly “finds order”: letter clouds slow, align, and begin converging toward center frame.

10–12s: Everything resolves cleanly into a centered final title that holds steady:
Seul astre exact un livre
The phrase is sharp for the first time, gently breathing with film weave; lens flare kisses the text as the sunbeam brightens behind it.

Sound design: faint projector whir + distant city hum + creaking metal + soft wind through broken panes. A barely whispered voiceover at the end reads the final phrase once (quiet, nostalgic), then cuts to silence as the title holds.”
